content: 1. Nutritional recovery and tuberculosis (TB) treatment outcomes in TB patients are influenced by the role of food assistance as a key enabler for adherence to treatment. The relative importance of food assistance compared to other enablers should be carefully evaluated. 2. Nutritional counseling can enhance the effectiveness and uptake of advice on nutritional outcomes. This is particularly important for pregnant women, both with and without TB, as their nutritional status impacts maternal and infant health outcomes. 3. The optimal body mass index (BMI) for healthy maternal and infant outcomes in pregnant women with TB should be determined and maintained. 4. A guiding principle in health care is a fundamental rule or assumption that directs care delivery. It is understood as an essential characteristic of health care and its intended purpose. Respecting these principles ensures effective use of health care services. 5. The Nutrition Guidance Advisory Group has identified five key guiding principles to assist national technical groups, international and regional partners, and TB care providers in formulating nutritional recommendations for TB patients. 6. All individuals with active TB should receive diagnosis, treatment, and care in accordance with WHO guidelines and international standards. This includes appropriate diagnostic procedures, support for treatment completion, and the provision of essential TB medications free of charge to minimize financial burdens. 7. Undernutrition identified at the time of TB diagnosis should be addressed as a key causal factor. Nutritional assessment and assistance should not divert resources from optimal TB diagnosis and care. 8. A well-balanced diet containing essential macroand micronutrients is necessary for the health and well-being of all individuals, including those with TB. Nutritional deficiencies impair immunity and increase susceptibility to infections, while infections exacerbate malnutrition. 9. Micronutrients such as vitamins A, C, D, E, B6, folic acid, and minerals like zinc, copper, selenium, and iron play critical roles in immune function and metabolic pathways. Their concentrations may influence an individual’s defense against TB. 10. Undernutrition is a significant contributor to active TB worldwide. Reducing undernutrition in the general population could substantially lower TB incidence. 11. Due to the bidirectional relationship between undernutrition and active TB, nutrition screening, assessment, and management are integral components of TB care. Many TB patients are undernourished at diagnosis, necessitating immediate nutritional assessment and intervention. 12. Nutritional assessment includes anthropometric, biochemical, clinical, and dietary evaluations. These assessments guide counseling and interventions throughout TB treatment. 13. Primary and community health-care workers play a vital role in nutrition screening, identifying undernourished patients, and providing further assessment and care. 14. At diagnosis, nutrition screening should include anthropometric and clinical measurements. If undernutrition is diagnosed, dietary assessment is also indicated. 15. Follow-up assessments during TB treatment should include weight, BMI calculations, and classification of nutritional status. Weight loss or failure to regain healthy weight should prompt further evaluation and intervention. 16. Nutritional counseling aims to improve dietary intake during recovery, support immune responses, repair damaged tissues, and manage TB drug side effects such as nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, and altered taste. 17. Practical advice on meeting macroand micronutrient requirements through locally available and culturally appropriate foods should be provided. 18. Poverty and food insecurity are both causes and consequences of TB. Addressing these socioeconomic issues is essential for effective TB care and control. 19. Food insecurity and poor nutritional status contribute to the global burden of active TB. Interventions addressing food security can improve treatment access, adherence, and nutritional recovery. 20. Food assistance may not always be the best enabler for TB treatment adherence or the most effective way to alleviate the economic and social costs of TB. Context-specific solutions should be considered. 21. TB programs should collaborate with food security and social protection services to ensure access to adequate food assistance and social benefits for TB patients and their families. 22. TB is often accompanied by comorbidities such as HIV, diabetes, smoking, and substance misuse, which have nutritional implications. These should be fully considered during nutrition screening, assessment, and counseling. 23. Addressing comorbid conditions improves nutritional status, access to TB treatment, and treatment outcomes. Nutritional counseling should be tailored to the specific needs of patients with comorbidities. 24. HIV increases the risk of active TB and undernutrition, particularly in regions with high HIV prevalence. Nutritional care for people living with HIV/AIDS is essential. 25. Diabetes mellitus triples the risk of developing TB and complicates its clinical course. TB can also make blood glucose management more challenging, necessitating careful clinical care for individuals with both conditions. 26. Early diagnosis of TB in people with diabetes and vice versa is critical for optimizing management of both diseases. Diet is a key component of diabetes management and should be included in nutritional counseling for TB patients. 27. All individuals with active TB should receive nutritional assessment and counseling at diagnosis and throughout treatment. 28. School-age children, adolescents, and adults with active TB and severe acute malnutrition should be treated according to WHO recommendations for managing severe acute malnutrition. 29. Children under five years of age with active TB and severe acute malnutrition should also be managed according to WHO guidelines for this age group. 30. Patients with moderate undernutrition who fail to regain normal BMI after two months of TB treatment or lose weight during treatment should be evaluated for adherence and comorbid conditions. They should receive nutritional assessment, counseling, and, if necessary, nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods. 31. Pregnant women with active TB and moderate undernutrition or inadequate weight gain should be provided with nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to achieve appropriate weight gain during pregnancy. 32. Patients with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and moderate undernutrition should receive nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to restore normal nutritional status. 33. In settings where fortified or supplementary foods are unavailable, daily multiple micronutrient supplements at recommended nutrient intake levels should be provided. 34. Pregnant women with active TB should receive multiple micronutrient supplements containing iron, folic acid, and other essential vitamins and minerals to meet maternal micronutrient needs. 35. In settings with low calcium intake, calcium supplementation should be provided to pregnant women with active TB.
